01.note: A purse of charity money arrived in the city of Pumbedita, and Rav Yosef deposited it with a certain man. The man was careless with it, and thieves came and stole it. Rav Yosef held him liable to pay. Abaye challenged him with a teaching that the bailee's duty covers money given to safeguard, not money given to distribute to the poor. Rav Yosef answered that the poor of Pumbedita each had a fixed sum set aside for them, so this money counted as money to safeguard, and the man had to pay.
01.why: The Gemara has just been asking when a bailee is responsible for an item that came into his possession for safeguarding rather than for some other purpose; this case tests that line with charity funds.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who deposited the charity purse with the man and ruled him liable when it was stolen.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenges Rav Yosef's ruling with a teaching about money meant for the poor.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one to challenge or support a ruling.
Someone entrusted with another person's property to look after; Jewish law sets out when he must pay if it is lost or stolen.

02.note: Rabbi Yohanan says a certain ruling dates from the days of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and cites a teaching to show it. A man who wanted to repent of his thieving was told by his wife: "Empty one! If you repent, even the belt you are wearing is not yours." He held back and did not repent. At that time the Sages declared that when robbers or lenders who took interest return what they took, it should not be accepted from them, and the Sages are displeased with anyone who does accept it.
02.why: The Gemara has just quoted this ruling as part of its discussion of the ordinance made to ease the way for those who repent; Rabbi Yohanan's story explains where the ruling came from. The Gemara then tests it against a teaching about children who inherit money taken as interest.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who dates the ruling and cites the story as its origin.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply "Rabbi"; the ruling was taught in his days.

terms.meaning: Lenders who charge interest; Torah law forbids Jews to take interest from one another, so such money must in principle be returned.
To turn back from wrongdoing; for a thief, true repentance includes returning what he stole.

03.note: A man robbed another of a pair of oxen, plowed and sowed his field with them, and eventually returned them. The owner came before Rav Nahman, who ordered that the increase in the land's value be estimated and paid. Rava objected that the land had improved partly on its own; Rav Nahman said he meant only half the increase. Rava pressed that a stolen item is simply returned as it was. Rav Nahman replied: Did I not tell you not to say anything to me while I sit in judgment? Our friend Huna said I am the equal of King Shapur in monetary law. This man is an old robber, and I want to penalize him.
03.why: The Gemara is explaining the mishna's principle that all robbers pay according to the value at the time of the robbery. Rava quotes that very rule, and Rav Nahman's reply shows a judge going beyond it to fine a habitual robber.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the robber to pay part of the land's increase in value, as a penalty.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Questions Rav Nahman's ruling while he is sitting in judgment.

people.name: Huna
people.about: Called "our friend" by Rav Nahman, who quotes him praising Rav Nahman's authority in monetary law.

terms.meaning: Here a nickname: the translation explains it as Shmuel, a leading authority on monetary law, so Rav Nahman is claiming equal standing with him.
A ruling from the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

04.note: Rav Yosef bar Hama's household would seize the slaves of people who owed him money and put them to work. His son Rabba asked why. Rav Yosef bar Hama cited Rav Nahman: a slave is not worth even the bread in his stomach. Rabba answered that Rav Nahman meant a slave like his own Daru, who only danced among the wine barrels; other slaves do real work. His father then cited Rav's ruling that one who seizes another's slave and works him owes nothing. Rabba replied that this holds only when no money is owed; for a creditor it looks like interest. Rav Yosef bar Hama said: I retract.
04.why: The Gemara has just argued that an owner is glad to have his slave kept working, so one who uses another's slave need not pay. The story shows the limit: when the user is the owner's creditor, the same use looks like interest.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: A creditor whose household put his debtors' slaves to work; he retracts when his son objects.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama, who questions his father's practice.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage quoted on both sides of the argument; Daru was his slave.

people.name: Daru
people.about: Rav Nahman's slave, who, Rabba says, only danced among the wine barrels.

people.name: Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina
people.about: Sage who reports Rav's ruling that one who works another's slave is exempt.

terms.meaning: Payment for the use of a loan. Torah law forbids Jews to take it from one another, and the Sages also forbade anything that merely looks like it, such as a creditor getting free labor from a debtor.

05.note: A woman showed a dinar coin to Rabbi Hiyya, who told her it was good. The next day she came back and said others had told her it was bad, and she could not spend it. Rabbi Hiyya told Rav to go and exchange it for her, and to write in his notebook: this was a bad transaction.
05.why: The Gemara has ruled that an expert money changer who misjudges a coin is exempt. It then asks why Rabbi Hiyya, himself an expert, paid, and answers that he acted beyond the letter of the law.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who judged the woman's coin to be good and then replaced it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Hiyya to exchange the coin and record the mistake.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.

06.note: Rav Kahana paid in advance for flax and left it with the seller. The price of flax rose, and the seller sold it. Rav Kahana came to Rav and asked whether he should go and take his money. Rav told him: if, when they sold it, they said "This flax is Kahana's," go and take it; if not, do not take it.
06.why: The Gemara has been discussing purchases made on someone else's behalf. It then asks whose view Rav's ruling follows, and concludes that the worry was that taking the higher price would look like interest on money paid in advance.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Paid in advance for flax, which the seller later sold after its price rose.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Kahana consulted about whether he could take the money.

terms.meaning: A plant grown for its fibers, which are spun into linen.

07.note: Rava tells of a pious man who bought something from one of two people and did not know which one. He came to Rabbi Tarfon, who told him to place the price between them and walk away. He then came to Rabbi Akiva, who told him he had no remedy until he paid each of them in full. Rava argues that a pious man would never have sworn a false oath.
07.why: The Gemara had suggested that Rabbi Akiva demands payment to every possible owner only from someone who swore falsely. Rava uses this pious buyer to challenge that limit, since Akiva made the same demand of him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sage who tells the incident to challenge an explanation of Rabbi Akiva's view.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: Tells the buyer to leave the price between the two sellers and walk away.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Tells the buyer he must pay each of the two sellers.

terms.meaning: A person known for strict and careful observance. The Gemara says that when it speaks of "a certain pious man" it means one of two Sages who were pious all their lives.
Swearing in court that something untrue is true, for example that one owes nothing. It is a serious sin and brings extra penalties.

08.note: Rabbi Abba was owed money by Rav Yosef bar Hama, and asked Rav Safra to bring it back with him. When Rav Safra arrived, Rava, Rav Yosef bar Hama's son, asked whether Rabbi Abba had given him a written receipt. He had not, so Rava told him to go and get one first. Then Rava changed his mind: even a receipt was worthless, since Rabbi Abba might die before Rav Safra returned, and the money would belong to his orphans. Rav Safra asked what could be done. Rava told him to have Rabbi Abba transfer the debt to him along with a piece of land, then come and write the receipt himself.
08.why: Shmuel has ruled that a debtor may not send payment through someone carrying the creditor's sign. The Gemara asks what a creditor can do under that rule, and this case gives the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Creditor who asks Rav Safra to collect his debt from Rav Yosef bar Hama.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: Owes money to Rabbi Abba; his son Rava handles the payment.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Abba to bring back the money.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rav Yosef bar Hama, who explains what Rav Safra needs before his father can pay him.

terms.meaning: The wording of a receipt in which a creditor confirms the debt was paid, protecting the debtor from being asked to pay again.
A legal device: rights that cannot be handed over on their own, such as a debt, are transferred together with a piece of land, which can be.

09.note: Rav Pappa was owed twelve thousand dinars by someone in Bei Hozai. He transferred his claim to Rav Shmuel bar Abba, together with the threshold of his house. When Rav Shmuel bar Abba came back with the money, Rav Pappa went out as far as Tavakh to meet him.
09.why: The Gemara has just explained that a creditor can collect through a messenger by transferring the debt to him together with land. Rav Pappa's case shows that method being used.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A creditor owed twelve thousand dinars, who transfers the debt to Rav Shmuel bar Abba to collect it.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Abba
people.about: Receives the claim and brings back the money.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.
A small piece of real estate. Handing it over lets the debt be transferred along with it, since land can carry other property with it in a transfer.

10.note: Rabbi Yirmeya's young brother-in-law, his wife's brother, shut the doors of his late father's house against Rabbi Yirmeya, who claimed part of it as his. Rabbi Yirmeya came before Rabbi Avin, who said the boy was claiming what was his. Rabbi Yirmeya said he could bring witnesses that he had taken possession during the father's lifetime. Rabbi Avin began to answer by asking whether a court accepts witnesses; the story breaks off there.
10.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that heirs, adults or minors, must return stolen goods they inherit, while Sumakhos exempts minors; this case raises how a court can hear a claim against a minor heir.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Claims part of his late father-in-law's house, which his young brother-in-law has shut him out of.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: The Sage Rabbi Yirmeya brings his claim to.

terms.meaning: Using or occupying property in a way that, under Jewish law, can establish ownership or support a claim to it.

10.flag: STORY ends mid-sentence (Rabbi Avin's question about accepting witnesses); the rest of the exchange, Sumakhos and Rabbi Abbahu, is in the AFTER segments and in story 34EE21.

11.note: Rabbi Yirmeya's dispute with his young brother-in-law over his late father-in-law's house reached Rabbi Abbahu. He asked whether they had not heard what Rav Yosef bar Hama said in Rabbi Oshaya's name: when a child takes his slaves into someone else's field and says "It is mine," the court does not wait until he grows up. It removes the field from him at once, and when he is grown he may bring witnesses and his claim will be examined.
11.why: Rabbi Avin had refused to hear witnesses against a minor; Rabbi Abbahu's ruling would let Rabbi Yirmeya win. The Gemara rejects the comparison: the boy holds the house from his father, unlike the child in Rabbi Oshaya's case.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the dispute finally reaches, who cites Rabbi Oshaya's ruling.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: Reports Rabbi Oshaya's ruling about a child who seizes a field.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about a child claiming a field Rabbi Abbahu cites.

terms.meaning: Present people who saw the relevant events to testify in court; here, the child may prove his claim once he is an adult.

11.flag: The story continues an incident begun in the BEFORE segments (story 44A855); Rabbi Yirmeya and his brother-in-law are not named inside the STORY segment itself.

12.note: Rav Asi visited Rav Kahana's house. He saw that Rav Kahana had summoned a certain woman to court in the evening, and by morning, when she had not come, had written a document banning her. Rav Asi asked whether he did not hold with Rav Hisda that a court sets dates on Monday, Thursday and Monday first. Rav Kahana replied that this is for a man, who may be away from town for reasons beyond his control. A woman is always in town, so if she does not come, she is rebellious.
12.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Hisda's rule of three court dates before a ban is written; this case tests that rule against Rav Kahana's quicker practice with a woman.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Visits Rav Kahana and questions his quick ban on a woman.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Judge who banned a woman the morning after she failed to appear.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose rule of three court dates Rav Asi cites.

terms.meaning: A court order placing someone under a ban, cutting them off from normal dealings with the community until they comply.
Here, someone who defies the court on purpose, as opposed to someone kept away by circumstances.

13.note: Rav Ashi was traveling on the road and saw clusters of grapes hanging on a vine in an orchard. He told his attendant to go and see whose they were: if they belonged to a gentile, bring some; if to a Jew, bring none. A gentile sitting in the orchard heard him and asked: Is it permitted to take from a gentile? Rav Ashi answered that a gentile takes money for his grapes, while a Jew does not.
13.why: The Gemara has been discussing what a Jew owes a gentile: returning lost items, and benefiting from a gentile's business mistakes. This is the last in a series of incidents on that theme.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Traveling Sage who wants to take grapes only if he can pay for them.

people.name: the gentile
people.about: Sitting in the orchard; he overhears Rav Ashi and challenges him.

terms.meaning: A person who is not Jewish.
A student or servant who travels with a Sage and runs errands for him.

14.note: Shmuel told of a man who said, just in passing, that he remembered being a small child riding on his father's shoulder. They took him from school, took off his tunic and immersed him so he could eat teruma, the priests' portion of produce, that evening. In Rabbi Hanina's telling he added: my friends kept away from me and called me "Yohanan, eater of hallot." On the strength of what he said, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi raised him to the priesthood.
14.why: Rav Ashi has said that remarks made in passing are relied on only for letting a woman remarry and in matters of rabbinic law. The Gemara cites this case against him, since eating teruma is a matter of Torah law.

people.name: Yohanan
people.about: The man whose memories of eating teruma as a child led to his acceptance as a priest.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply "Rabbi"; he raised Yohanan to the priesthood on the strength of his words.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Sage who adds the ending about the friends' nickname.

terms.meaning: Mentioning a fact in passing, without trying to prove anything. Such remarks are sometimes trusted even from people who could not testify formally in court.
Dipped in a ritual bath to become ritually pure, which a priest must be before eating teruma.
The portion of dough given to priests. Like teruma, only priests may eat it.
The status of being a kohen, a descendant of Aaron, with rights such as eating teruma.

15.note: Rav Huna was a student of Rav. A thief known as Hanan the Wicked stole a cloak and sold it. When the case came before Rav Huna, he told the man whose cloak was stolen: Go redeem your pledge, meaning pay back the buyer and take the cloak.
15.why: Rav has said that the Sages did not apply the marketplace rule here, so a buyer can recover his money only from the thief. The Gemara cites this ruling by Rav's own student against that, then answers that Hanan, who had no money, was a special case.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A student of Rav who judged the case of the stolen cloak.

people.name: Hanan the Wicked
people.about: A thief who stole a cloak and sold it.

terms.term: provision ensuring the integrity of the marketplace
terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: when a stolen item is found with someone who bought it in good faith, the owner must repay the buyer's price to get it back, so that ordinary buying and selling stays safe.

16.note: Avimi bar Nazi, Ravina's father-in-law, was owed four dinars by a man. The man stole a cloak and brought it to him, and Avimi then lent him four more dinars. In the end the man was found to be the thief, and the case came before Ravina. He ruled that for the first four dinars the owner owes Avimi nothing, but for the four later dinars Avimi should take his money from the owner and return the cloak.
16.why: The Gemara has just ruled that the marketplace ordinance protects buyers of stolen goods, but not a creditor repaid with stolen goods. Ravina applies that line to a case with both kinds of loan; Rav Kohen objects and Rabbi Abbahu rules with him.

people.name: Avimi bar Nazi
people.about: Ravina's father-in-law, who lent money to a man who brought him a stolen cloak.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The judge who splits the case between the two loans.

terms.meaning: A silver coin in common use at the time.

terms.term: ordinance ensuring the integrity of the marketplace
terms.meaning: A rule of the Sages that an owner must repay a good-faith buyer before taking back a stolen item, so that ordinary trade stays safe.

17.note: A man from Naresh stole a scroll and sold it to a man from Pappunya for eighty dinars, who sold it on to a man from Mehoza for one hundred and twenty. In the end the thief was identified. Abaye ruled that the owner should pay the man from Mehoza eighty dinars and take back his scroll, and the man from Mehoza should collect the other forty from the man from Pappunya. Rava objected: if the Sages protect someone who buys from a thief, surely they protect someone who buys from a buyer.
17.why: The Gemara is working through how far the marketplace ordinance protects buyers of stolen goods; this case asks about a second buyer. Rava then rules that the owner pays the full 120 and recovers it from the two sellers.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rules that the owner repays only the eighty dinars the thief received.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Objects that a second buyer deserves the same protection as the first.

terms.meaning: A handwritten book on parchment, such as a Torah scroll; very valuable at the time.

terms.term: provision ensuring the integrity of the marketplace
terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: the owner of a stolen item must repay a good-faith buyer's price to get it back, so that ordinary trade stays safe.

17.flag: STORY ends with Rava's objection; his own ruling, which resolves the case, is in the next segment (AFTER).

18.note: Rav Safra was traveling with a caravan, and a lion followed along with them. Every night the travelers sent the lion one of their donkeys, and it ate it. When Rav Safra's turn came, he sent his donkey, but the lion did not eat it. Rav Safra hurried and took it back as his own.
18.why: Rav has just ruled that someone who sets out to rescue another's donkey on the promise of payment is still paid if his own donkey comes out of the river by itself: mercy came to him from Heaven. Rav Safra's donkey is compared to that case.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A traveler in a caravan whose donkey the lion did not eat.

terms.meaning: A group of travelers journeying together for safety, with their pack animals.
Took formal ownership. Having given the donkey up to the lion, Rav Safra treated it as ownerless and took possession of it again.

19.note: A man showed thugs where the Exilarch's household kept its piles of wheat, and they seized them. Rav Nahman ruled that the man must pay. Rav Huna bar Hiyya, seated before him, with Rav Yosef behind, asked whether this was the law or a fine. Rav Nahman said it was the law, from the mishna about one who showed a field to thugs. After he left, Rav Yosef asked Rav Huna bar Hiyya why it mattered. He answered: if it is the law, we learn from it for other cases; if it is a fine, we do not.
19.why: The mishna has just ruled that one whose actions caused thugs to seize a field must replace it, and the Gemara explained this as a case of showing them the field. This case applies that reading and asks whether such rulings set precedent.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who orders the man to pay for the wheat.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Seated before Rav Nahman; asks whether the ruling was law or a fine.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Seated behind Rav Huna bar Hiyya; later asks him why the question mattered.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official with his own household and estates.
A penalty a court imposes to deter wrongdoing, beyond what the strict law requires; a fine in one case does not set a rule for others.
A ruling from the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

20.note: Gentiles forced a man to show them the wine of Rav Mari, son of Rav Pinehas, son of Rav Hisda. Then they told him to carry it and bring it along with them, and he did. The case came before Rav Ashi, who exempted him from paying. The Rabbis objected that a teaching makes one who hands property over with his own hands liable. Rav Ashi answered that this applies only when he did not lead them to the property at the start. Once he had, it was as if the wine were already burned.
20.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that one forced to show property to gentiles is exempt, but one who hands it over himself is liable. This case falls between the two, and Rav Ashi draws the line.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: Son of Rav Pinehas, son of Rav Hisda; the owner of the wine the gentiles took.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The judge who exempts the man from paying for the wine.

terms.meaning: People who are not Jewish; here, men who coerce a Jew into helping them seize property.
Here, the scholars present with Rav Ashi, who question his ruling.
